title: Agentic AI: Three Operator Cases
points: Understand the problem, follow the agent and review the evidence.
90 minutes / three what-if discussions
note: The examples are self-contained. No computer or software setup is needed. We will follow a goal, the agent’s requests, numerical evidence and a human decision. The results come from reduced or synthetic studies; they are examples for learning.

title: An agent chooses what to try next
points: Give the agent a goal. It requests a tool, reads the result and chooses the next step.
note: The agent does not calculate the electrical result by writing a confident answer. It chooses a permitted tool, reads the result and decides whether another request or human review is needed. Trace the feedback arrow once with the audience.
caption: Teaching diagram: the model requests a tool and uses the returned evidence.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.2.

title: The agent asks; the tool calculates
points: A tool does one job. An agent can connect several jobs using their results.
note: The Stanford figure distinguishes one function call from a longer agentic workflow. A function can perform one calculation. An agentic workflow connects requests and uses returned results to decide what comes next.
caption: Original Stanford figure: one function call and a multi-step workflow.
image_credit: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.2.

title: Solar settings: which option should we try?
points: Compare possible settings, then check voltage and line current.
The agent can organize these trials and report the checked options.
caption: The tool calculates; the agent coordinates the next request.
note: Suppose an operator needs new solar settings. Different settings affect voltage, current and useful solar output. The agent organizes a bounded study; the numerical tool supplies the engineering evidence.

title: Give the agent a goal and clear limits
points: State the goal, allowed tools and stopping rules.
Keep the operator’s review step explicit.
note: A useful request states the operating goal, available tools and stopping conditions. The agent needs to know when it must ask for review rather than continue trying options. The operator defines these boundaries.
caption: Grid teaching adaptation of Stanford’s task-specification concept.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.40.

title: Restoration: who should get power first?
points: The operator sets the service priority.
That priority changes the study the agent requests.
caption: Same network and limits, different service goals.
note: When supply is limited, restoring the greatest total power can differ from protecting essential services. The operator chooses that priority. The agent must preserve it when requesting and comparing studies.

title: Keep three jobs clear
points: The agent requests a study. The tool calculates. The operator reviews the result.
source_label: Monica Lam. CS224V Agentic AI, Lecture 1: Introduction. Stanford University, Fall 2026, p.53.
note: Keep the jobs separate. The agent coordinates requests. The numerical tool calculates. The operator reviews the evidence and decides the next authorized step. A tool passing its checks is not operating permission.
caption: Adapted principle: language, calculation and human review have different jobs.

title: Wrong readings can still fit a model
points: A good fit alone does not prove that the readings are true.
The agent can organize checks and flag missing evidence.
caption: Model fit and trusted information answer different questions.
note: Readings may fit a model and still be wrong. An alarm test measures one kind of mismatch. The agent can request additional checks and identify missing information, but its explanation cannot make a data source trustworthy.

title: Case 1: which solar settings should we use?
points: Use solar generation while keeping voltage and line current within the allowed range.
An agent can organize the trials and return checked options.
note: Start with the physical problem: choose solar controls that respect voltage, current and equipment capacity while serving the stated generation goal. The agent can organize trials and return a checked option. It does not replace the solver or the operator.
caption: Concept sketch: choose settings, then calculate their effects.

title: Two tools suggest different settings
points: MPC plans with a model. SAC uses a previously trained controller.
Treat both outputs as proposals that need the same electrical checks.
note: MPC means model predictive control: it plans with a model. SAC means soft actor-critic: it uses a previously trained policy. Both produce proposals. Apply the same electrical checks to each before comparing cost or usefulness.
caption: MPC: model predictive control. SAC: soft actor-critic. Both proposals need the same checks.

title: How the agent helps with solar settings
points: The agent requests a study and reads the returned checks.
It can try another allowed option or ask the operator for help.
note: Read the loop from left to right. The operator supplies a goal. The agent requests an allowed trial. The tool calculates voltage and current. The checks decide whether it can be compared. A failed trial can lead to another permitted request or a request for help.
caption: The agent uses returned checks to choose the next permitted step.

title: Two solar settings change the result
points: One setting controls solar power output. The other provides voltage support.
The tool checks voltage, line current and the solar unit’s capacity.
note: The two controls are active-power output and voltage support. The source model represents them as a and b. They share inverter capacity, so reducing one effect can change another. Use the tool to calculate those effects rather than infer safety from the control names.
caption: Active power and voltage support share equipment capacity.

title: Both proposals face the same checks
points: The tool calculates the effect of each proposal.
Compare their scores only after voltage, current and capacity checks pass.
note: The same checks apply to both candidates. Check voltage, line current and inverter capacity first. Only a passing proposal is eligible for cost comparison. The agent’s next request should be based on the returned checks.
caption: Both proposals need the same voltage, current and capacity checks.

title: Read the voltage and current checks
points: Left: voltages should stay in the allowed band.
Right: current should stay below 100% of the allowance.
note: The left plot shows the voltage distribution. The right compares current use with the allowed current. Both pass this model’s checks. The curves on the left are sorted separately, so their horizontal rank is not a matched physical location.
caption: Calculated example at the original current allowance.

title: Both pass, but the trade-off is different
points: MPC uses 73.62% of the current allowance; SAC uses 51.68%.
MPC has the lower overall score because current is only one part of the goal.
note: The current-use values are 73.62% for MPC and 51.68% for saved SAC. Their scores are approximately 0.03110 and 0.43643. Lower score is preferred after all checks pass. SAC uses less current here partly because it also uses less active power.
caption: Calculated example: both electrical checks pass.

title: What if we allow less current?
points: Reduce the allowance from 80% to 75% of nominal current.
Which proposal might fail? Which would you choose if both pass?
What must the agent ask the tool to check again?
note: Ask people to predict without doing any calculation. Make the rule change explicit: allowed current decreases from 80% to 75% of nominal. Give pairs time to explain what must be checked again and why the lowest current is not automatically the best proposal. Advance only after the discussion.
caption: Discuss the scenario, then advance to the calculated result.

title: Both proposals pass the new current check
points: MPC has the lower score. SAC uses less current and less solar output.
These results cover the medium-voltage model. A wider grid needs a wider study.
note: The numerical study has already been calculated for this changed allowance. MPC uses about 78.53% of the new allowance and SAC about 54.85%; both pass. Their scores are about 0.03110 and 0.43246. MPC has the lower score. These checks cover the medium-voltage model, not the entire distribution system.
caption: Same load; the allowed current has been reduced to 75% of nominal.
answer_for: What if we allow less current?

title: Less current does not mean the best option
points: Here SAC also uses less solar output.
The operator’s goal values solar generation as well as operating limits.
note: In the changed-allowance example, the active-power setting is about 96% of inverter rating for MPC and 34% for SAC. These percentages use inverter rating as the base. Less current comes with a generation trade-off, so the operator’s objective matters.
caption: Active-power settings use inverter rating as their base.

title: A PASS covers only the checked model
points: A study of the medium-voltage network cannot confirm a whole-grid claim.
The agent should request the missing study or return HOLD.
note: The model’s scope travels with its result. A passing medium-voltage study does not establish low-voltage or whole-feeder safety. When the request is wider than the evidence, the useful response is a missing-study request or HOLD.
caption: A passing result applies to the model and conditions actually checked.

title: Recorded example: the first option fails
points: Llama requests a check of the saved SAC proposal.
The numerical tool reports too much current and rejects it.
note: This is a separate recorded full-feeder study, with different inputs from the earlier numerical comparison. Read the actual Llama request and returned tool result. The SAC trial reaches about 111.97% of allowed current, so it fails. The tool result determines eligibility.
caption: Recorded full-feeder study; different inputs from the earlier comparison.

title: Recorded example: another option is checked
points: Llama requests a check of the existing MPC fallback.
The returned electrical checks pass for this recorded case.
note: The agent requests a check of an existing MPC fallback. It does not invent or solve MPC. The historical electrical check returns about 99.60% of allowed current and no listed violations. That makes the option eligible for review within this study’s stated scope.
caption: Recorded full-feeder study: the requested fallback passes the checks.

title: Recorded example: the operator receives a proposal
points: The agent returns the checked proposal and its conditions.
The operator still reviews it before any authorized action.
note: The recorded workflow returns the checked proposal, while human acknowledgement remains pending and no equipment command is sent. Ask what evidence the operator receives and what remains outside the study, including permissions and protection checks.
caption: Recorded workflow result; human review remains pending.

title: Case 2: who gets power after a fault?
points: A fault removes a supply path. Available capacity limits what can be restored.
The operator sets priorities; the agent can request and check restoration options.
note: A fault removes one supply path in the six-node network. The available backup capacity limits which loads can be restored. Cyan marks the critical loads. The operator defines priorities, while the agent can request alternative restoration studies.
caption: Six-node example. Cyan marks critical loads; dashed links are backup paths.

title: How the agent helps restore service
points: Choose the goal: critical loads first, or the most total power.
The agent can request a study, read the trade-off and ask for a new study when limits change.
note: The goal changes the requested optimization. The agent should keep the operator’s priority, ask the tool for a plan, read service and capacity checks, and request a new study when inputs change. The solver decides which whole loads fit the network constraints.
caption: The operator sets the priority. The agent requests the matching study.

title: The service goal changes the study request
points: Critical-first gives more weight to essential service.
Most-total-power aims to restore the largest amount of power.
note: Critical-first assigns more value to essential service. Most-total-power maximizes total restored kW. Both still need the same network constraints. The agent translates the selected goal into the appropriate permitted study request; the solver performs the optimization.
caption: Two possible operator goals for the same fault and available network.

title: The goal changes who receives power
points: Critical-first: 130 kW total, including 90 kW for critical loads.
Most-total-power: 140 kW total, including 30 kW for critical loads.
note: At a 40 kW backup tie, the critical-first result restores 130 kW total, including 90 kW critical. The total-power result restores 140 kW, including only 30 kW critical. Neither objective removes the need to explain the service trade-off. In the plots, overlapping markers indicate equal outcomes.
caption: Calculated restoration results for the same network and limits.

title: Check the restoration plan
points: Keep the faulted branch out of service. Check supply paths and capacity.
Voltage, protection and field switching need separate studies.
note: Check that the fault stays isolated, supply paths connect and capacities are respected. This teaching exercise uses an active-power service model. AC voltages, protection coordination and the order of physical switching require separate studies and procedures.
caption: Active-power model checks. Voltage, protection and field switching require separate work.

title: What if the backup path can carry more power?
points: Increase its capacity from 40 kW to 180 kW. Keep the fault and loads the same.
Would the two service goals still give different results?
What should the agent recalculate before reporting the new plan?
note: Change only backup capacity in the scenario, from 40 to 180 kW. Ask whether the two service goals must always disagree. Invite participants to explain what the agent should recalculate before presenting a new plan. No software is needed to make the prediction.
caption: Discuss the scenario, then advance to the calculated result.

title: More capacity removes this service trade-off
points: At 40 kW, critical-first serves 90 kW of critical load instead of 30 kW.
At 180 kW, both goals serve 250 kW total, including all 90 kW of critical load.
note: At 180 kW the two goals both restore 250 kW total, including 90 kW critical. Among the sampled capacities, the first agreement is at 80 kW. That discrete sweep does not establish an exact continuous crossover. More capacity removes the trade-off in this example.
caption: Calculated results with the same fault, loads and service goals.
answer_for: What if the backup path can carry more power?

title: A new limit needs a new study
points: Now reduce the allowed backup capacity from 40 kW to 20 kW.
The old result no longer supports the request. The agent must request a new study.
note: Now imagine a stricter request: the backup capacity falls from 40 to 20 kW. Evidence calculated for the old capacity no longer matches the request. The agent should hold the old proposal and obtain a new constrained study. A failed evidence match does not itself prove that every new plan will fail.
caption: A changed limit requires evidence calculated for the new request.

title: The agent keeps the operator’s goal
points: The operator sets priorities. The solver selects loads.
The agent can request the solve and explain the returned service trade-off.
note: In the illustrated priority plan, loads 1, 2 and 5 receive service: 130 kW total and 90 kW critical. The operator sets the goal. The numerical solver selects loads. The agent can request the solve and explain the returned trade-off without changing the goal.
caption: The operator’s priority stays fixed while the tool selects a feasible plan.

title: Recorded example: another plan restores more service
points: In this separate larger-feeder study, Llama requests another plan.
The tool reports more service and passing electrical checks.
note: This recorded larger-feeder example is separate from the six-node illustration. Llama requests another catalog option. The tool returns about 1,843.61 kW total and 474.04 kW critical service, with current at about 91.87% of its allowance. A proposed improvement becomes evidence only after the check.
caption: Recorded larger-feeder example, separate from the six-node network.

title: Recorded example: the tool rejects a trial
points: The next trial carries too much current.
It cannot replace the previous passing option.
note: The next recorded trial restores more load but reaches about 111.01% of allowed current. It is rejected. The agent must keep the earlier passing option eligible rather than replace it with an overloaded plan.
caption: Recorded larger-feeder example: the overloaded trial is rejected.

title: Recorded example: a wrong ranking is corrected
points: Llama puts two passing plans in the wrong cost order.
Python keeps the lower-cost plan and checks it again.
note: The model ranks two passing plans in the wrong cost order. Since smaller cost is preferred, negative 6109 is lower than negative 5509. Python keeps the lower-cost passing plan and rechecks it. This example shows why the workflow needs a numerical guard.
caption: Recorded larger-feeder example. Lower cost is preferred, including negative costs.

title: Case 3: can we trust these readings?
points: Wrong readings can still look consistent with the model.
The agent can request checks, but action still needs a trusted basis.
note: Wrong measurements can look consistent with a grid model. The operating question is whether the evidence supports a correction, not whether the agent can write a convincing explanation. Data trust and model coverage remain explicit conditions.
caption: Concept sketch using a small four-bus model.

title: How the agent helps with suspicious readings
points: The agent can request the checks and keep missing evidence visible.
The operator reviews trust, model coverage and the proposed correction.
note: The agent can request the permitted checks, read the results and report missing evidence. A required missing trust condition should lead to HOLD. The operator reviews the data basis, model scope and proposed adjustment.
caption: The agent requests checks and preserves missing evidence.

title: Mismatch is only one check
points: Mismatch J measures how well the model fits the readings.
The simulation lets us measure how wrong the estimate is (state error).
note: Mismatch J measures how well the model fits the readings. It is different from the control-cost score used in the solar case. The simulation also supplies a known true state, allowing an estimation error to be measured. That true state is not normally available to a real operator.
caption: Mismatch measures model fit; state error measures estimation accuracy.

title: Two patterns of wrong readings
points: One wrong reading may conflict with the other readings.
Coordinated changes may still look consistent with the model.
note: One biased reading can disagree with the remaining data. Coordinated changes can agree with one another and still move the estimated state away from truth. This is a conceptual illustration of the two tested patterns; it is not an instruction for creating an attack.
caption: Concept illustration of two patterns used in the numerical comparison.

title: Read the alarm and the estimation error
points: Left: mismatch and its alarm threshold. Right: error against the simulation’s known truth.
A quiet alarm can appear alongside a growing error.
note: The left plot compares mismatch with the alarm threshold. The right compares the state estimate with known simulation truth. A quiet alarm can coexist with a growing error. The agent should preserve this distinction when summarizing results.
caption: Calculated model-fit and state-error results.

title: A coordinated change can escape the alarm
points: At scale 1, one biased reading gives mismatch J=277.50 and an alarm.
A coordinated change gives J=3.92, no alarm, and 0.02678 rad of state error.
note: At the reference change size, an isolated bias gives mismatch about 277.50 and triggers the alarm. A coordinated change gives about 3.92, no alarm, and about 0.02678 radians of state error. A low mismatch is incomplete evidence about data trust.
caption: The known state is available inside the simulation for this comparison.

title: What if the data change is small?
points: Reduce the change to one tenth of the reference size.
Will the alarm always detect the error?
What else would the operator need before trusting the readings?
note: Ask pairs to predict what a smaller error does to the alarm. Use one tenth of the reference change size. The question is whether a quiet alarm proves correct readings and what independent information an operator would need. Reveal the calculated example on the next slide.
caption: Discuss the scenario, then advance to the calculated result.

title: A quiet alarm can still hide an error
points: Neither example triggers this alarm at one tenth of the reference size.
Both estimates still contain error. No alarm alone does not establish data trust.
note: For the smaller change, mismatch is about 10.14 for isolated bias and 3.92 for the coordinated pattern. Both are below the threshold of about 15.09. Both estimates still contain error. No alarm means this test has not crossed its threshold; it does not authenticate the readings.
caption: Calculated results at one tenth of the reference change size.
answer_for: What if the data change is small?

title: Trusted information is needed before recovery
points: Without the required trusted readings, the response is HOLD.
With readings assumed trustworthy, the tool can calculate a proposal for review.
note: The recovery example assumes additional trustworthy readings are available. Without that required condition the result is HOLD. With the assumption, the tool can calculate a bounded proposal. Neither the fitting algorithm nor Llama authenticates those channels.
caption: Additional trustworthy readings are assumed in this example.

title: The tool calculates a small correction
points: The solver finds the smallest allowed adjustment that meets the checked branch limits.
Predicted flow: 0.17000 p.u. Offline check: 0.17046 p.u. Limit: 0.18000 p.u.
note: The fixed recovery example proposes an adjustment of about 0.121694 per unit. The model predicts a monitored flow of 0.17000, while the offline synthetic-truth check gives 0.17046; both are below the 0.18000 limit. Per unit expresses values relative to a common model base. The offline truth check is an experimental aid, not guaranteed field information.
caption: Per-unit values share the same model base.

title: Recorded example: request the recovery tool
points: Llama requests the supplied recovery tool.
Python calculates a correction using the assumed trusted readings.
note: Read the actual recorded Llama request. The task already supplies a permitted recovery tool and the trusted-reading assumption. Python estimates the state and calculates the correction. The language model routes the request; it does not provide the numerical estimate.
caption: Recorded recovery request and numerical tool result.
image_transformation: Presentation selection of verified recorded fields. Exact returned reason is unchanged. Full data, hashes and source paths: research/llama_replay/episodes.json.

title: Recorded example: keep human review
points: The model checks pass; human review is still pending.
Data trust and operating permission still need review.
note: The recorded model checks pass, but the overall result remains REVIEW and human acknowledgement is pending. The operator still needs a trusted data basis and operating authority. The fixed workflow obtains the same numerical correction, so this is not evidence that Llama improves estimation.
caption: Recorded workflow result; human review remains pending.

title: Review must refer to the same proposal
points: The proposal ID and model scope must match the checked study.
A different proposal or wider scope needs a new review.
note: A reviewer must refer to the same proposal and scope that were checked. A changed proposal ID or a wider request cannot inherit an earlier passing result. In the teaching example, readback is simulated and sends no equipment command.
caption: Illustrative proposal IDs. Review is separate from equipment operation.

title: The operator chooses the next step
points: Review the case, tool results, checked limits and missing work.
Request another study, reject the proposal or take the next authorized step.
note: The operator can request more evidence, reject the proposal or continue with a defined authorized step. Review the case, returned limits, model coverage and missing studies. Acceptance of a study is separate from issuing a field command.
caption: The operator reviews the study and chooses the next authorized step.

title: Multi-agent framework used in these cases
points: The five roles share the same case facts and checked results.
One Llama model handles planning and refinement. Python calculates and checks.
note: Awareness reads the shared case. Planning prepares permitted options and uses Llama to choose a study. Simulation calculates. Verification checks limits and case identity. The Llama optimizer requests a bounded change or ranks passing options. Every changed trial returns for simulation and verification. Python guards the final choice before operator review. One Llama model fills two roles; this is not five independent language models. The implementation uses case-specific numerical tools behind the same stages.
caption: Implemented five-role workflow with a case-specific numerical tool.

title: Explain one case in your own words
points: What is the operator’s problem, and what should the agent request next?
Which tool result supports the proposal, and what must the operator still decide?
note: Ask participants to choose one case and explain the complete loop in their own words. They should name the problem, an agent request, a returned numerical fact and a remaining human decision. Optional practice materials can be used after the concept tutorial, but no account or code is needed for this discussion.
caption: Explain the idea first. Practice material is available separately.
